verified.title: email_retry_failed has no write-back and re-sends the same failed rows for a full 24h — CONFIRMED, and a since-merged 'fix' does not actually close the hole for the email template that caused the incident
verified.evidence: I read lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:71-104 myself. retryFailedEmails() does exactly what is claimed: SELECT * FROM email_logs WHERE status='failed' AND created_at in a [now-24h, now-5min] window ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50, then calls sendTemplatedEmail() per row inside a try/catch that on failure does nothing but `continue` — there is no UPDATE, no retry-count column, no write-back of any kind, so a still-failing row is eligible again on the very next 5-minute tick and stays eligible until it ages out of the 24h window. A sibling verifier (docs/audits/optimization-2026-09/verified/background-job-engine-lib-jobs-pg-cron-t.json, live prod re-query 2026-09-05) independently confirms this from the data side: 'EXACTLY SIX rows' for (to, template_key) pairs in 24h, with ezrawafula98@gmail.com/group_verification_link at 721 attempts, 163 actually delivered, and confirms the amplification mechanism (each failed retry mints a fresh 'failed' row via the SMTP adapter's queued-then-failed INSERT/UPDATE pair) with pg_stat_user_tables numbers (n_tup_ins 48,264 on email_logs). This is the same incident the finder describes (763/194 vs the sibling's 721/163 — the gap is normal drift between two snapshots taken days apart, not a discrepancy in the underlying bug). SELF-DERIVED ADDITION, not in the finder's or sibling's evidence: I traced whether a 2026-09-09 commit (749eb16, 'Prevent duplicate Resend emails with idempotency', merged to main, still present at HEAD) closes this. It adds an application-level pre-send dedup check plus a Resend idempotencyKey to lib/email/adapters/resend.ts:33-76 — but BOTH are gated on `payload.referenceType && payload.referenceId` being present. I checked the actual call site that sends this exact template: lib/services/group-verification.service.ts:72-83 calls sendTemplatedEmail({templateKey:'group_verification_link', to, vars, groupId}) — no referenceId, no referenceType. So `reference` is null in resend.ts, the dedup SELECT is skipped entirely, and idempotencyKey is null too (Resend's own dedup is also not engaged). The email_logs row that gets stored therefore has reference_id/reference_type = NULL, and retryFailedEmails() passes those same NULLs through on every retry. The 2026-09-09 commit is real and does add protection for OTHER templates that populate referenceId/referenceType, but the specific template responsible for the 194/163-duplicate incident is not covered by it — the vulnerability is still live in the code as of today.
verified.impact: A single real recipient can still receive on the order of hundreds of duplicate verification emails in a session because the loop that caused it (retryFailedEmails, unchanged) feeds a send path (group_verification_link) that the one dedup mechanism added since does not reach. The provider-quota-exhaustion mechanism (every retry attempt counts against the daily send quota regardless of whether it succeeds) is untouched by the September fix for any template, since the fix only prevents re-delivery of an already-succeeded send, not the repeated attempt itself.
verified.recommendation: Two independent fixes are both still needed. (1) The finder's fix: add a retry_attempted_at or retry_count column to email_logs, stamp it in retryFailedEmails(), and filter the SELECT on it, converting the unbounded loop into at-most-N. (2) Pass referenceType/referenceId at the group-verification call site (lib/services/group-verification.service.ts:72-83) — e.g. referenceType:'group_verification', referenceId: the verification row's id — so the September dedup fix actually covers this path the way it already covers others. Do (1) first; it is the root cause and fixes every template, including ones that will never carry a reference id.
verified.note: CONFIRMED at the code level by my own read, and on magnitude by an independent live-SQL re-verification from 2026-09-05 (a different verifier, same production database) that reproduced the same six-recipient/template pairs and the same order-of-magnitude counts. I additionally traced a since-merged partial fix and confirmed it does not cover the specific template that caused the reported harm — this is new information not present in the raw finding.

verified.title: email_send / the SMTP fallback costs ~31-32s per attempt because nodemailer's SMTP transport is created with no timeout options and defaults to a 30s greeting timeout
verified.evidence: I read lib/email/adapters/smtp.ts:6-16 myself: `nodemailer.createTransport({host, port, secure, auth})` — no connectionTimeout, greetingTimeout, or socketTimeout keys anywhere in the object, so nodemailer's built-in default (greetingTimeout=30000ms) governs. I also read lib/email/provider.ts:60-77: sendEmailWithFallback calls the primary adapter (Resend) and, only on failure, falls back to `new SmtpAdapter().send(payload)` when `process.env.SMTP_HOST` is set — matching the finder's description of a 'dead SMTP fallback'. I independently re-read app/api/cron/route.ts:38 (`maxDuration = 60`) and lib/jobs/processor.ts:72/:86 (`TIME_BUDGET_MS = 50_000`, `MIN_JOB_BUDGET_MS = 10_000`) — both match the finder's citation exactly, including the line numbers. A sibling verifier independently re-aggregated job_logs for this exact cost on live prod (2026-09-05): 'email_send/retried n=92 mean 32,254ms ... email_send/failed n=22 mean 32,259ms ... email_send/completed n=2 mean 1,122ms', all with error 'Greeting never received' — a weighted average of ~31,718ms across those 116 rows, which lines up with the finder's own job_logs aggregate of 104 rows at avg 31,705ms almost exactly (two independent snapshots, taken on different days, agreeing to within 0.05%). The mechanism (30s default greeting timeout, no override) fully explains this figure independently of any measurement.
verified.impact: Confirmed as described: any tick that draws an email_send (or email_retry_failed, which shares the same underlying sendTemplatedEmail -> SMTP-fallback path) job against a dead SMTP endpoint loses roughly 31-32 seconds of its ~40s effective working budget (TIME_BUDGET_MS minus MIN_JOB_BUDGET_MS) to a socket that structurally cannot answer, crowding out the other ~10-12 pending types competing for the same tick.
verified.recommendation: Same as the finder's: pass connectionTimeout/greetingTimeout/socketTimeout (e.g. 5000/5000/10000ms) to nodemailer.createTransport in smtp.ts:7, so a dead endpoint costs ~5s instead of ~30s. Independently, either fix or remove the SMTP_HOST env var so provider.ts:71 stops selecting a fallback that a sibling audit measured at 0 successes out of 554+ attempts in 48h.
verified.note: Confirmed both structurally (I read the exact code that produces a 30s default timeout with no override) and numerically (two independent live-data snapshots, mine cross-referenced against a sibling verifier's, agree to within a fraction of a percent).

verified.title: Six 5-minute sweeps use time-bucketed dedup keys and mint a new job_queue row every tick regardless of whether the previous one ever ran
verified.evidence: I read lib/jobs/index.ts in full myself. All six citations check out exactly: email_campaign_process (:62-65), email_retry_failed (:67-70), email_campaign_drain (:76-79), mpesa_reconcile (:133-136), mpesa_replay_callbacks (:139-142), outbox_dispatch (:145-148) all carry `dedup_key: \`${type}:${dateStr}T${hour}:${fiveMinBucket}\``, which changes every 5 minutes. The four converted siblings (sms_retry_failed :111-114, sms_process_schedules :116-119, sms_poll_dlr :121-124, sms_release_stale_reservations :128-131) carry bare constant dedup_keys exactly as claimed, and the comment at :107-110 stating the mpesa/outbox sweeps were 'Deliberately NOT applied ... not changed blind' is present verbatim. I also confirmed the enforcing mechanism directly from the migration: supabase/migrations/20260526120000_041_job_queue.sql:69-72 creates `idx_job_queue_dedup ON job_queue (dedup_key) WHERE dedup_key IS NOT NULL AND status NOT IN ('completed','failed')` — a constant key really does cap a type at one outstanding row. A sibling verifier independently confirmed the live consequence on 2026-09-05: the same six types held 19,729 pending rows (email_retry_failed 4,683, email_campaign_drain 3,731, email_campaign_process 3,692, mpesa_reconcile 2,897, mpesa_replay_callbacks 2,528, outbox_dispatch 2,198), every one payload-identical, versus the four converted types holding 0-1 row each — a 'one-to-one correlation with no exceptions' in their words. That backlog and its daily growth rate (they measured 1,728 junk rows/day) closely matches this finding's own 1,722/day figure — both independent measurements of the same live phenomenon, taken days apart.
verified.impact: Confirmed as the dominant driver of job_queue's size and of the claim-scan costs described elsewhere in this dimension. The daily 1,700+ row growth against a much smaller completion rate is corroborated by an independent live count within days of this audit.
verified.recommendation: Same as the finder's: change the six dedup_key expressions to bare constants exactly as lines 111-131 already do, then a one-off DELETE of the resulting orphaned pending rows.
verified.note: Fully confirmed: every code citation matched on my own read, and the live-data magnitude was independently reproduced by a different verifier against the same production database within the same week.

verified.title: pg_net's client-side timeout (20s) is well under the function's real budget (50-60s), so every cron HTTP response is discarded as a timeout while cron.job_run_details falsely reports 100% success
verified.evidence: The cron.schedule(...) call that sets `timeout_milliseconds := 20000` is not in the repo (DEPLOY.md:170-191 documents it as a manual Supabase SQL Editor step, matching the migration's own comment in 042_enable_pg_cron.sql that scheduling is 'a runtime config step ... not a migration'), so I could not read that literal value from source myself this session. I did independently confirm the two values it is being compared against: app/api/cron/route.ts:38 `maxDuration = 60` and lib/jobs/processor.ts:72 `TIME_BUDGET_MS = 50_000`, both exact matches to the finder's citation, including line numbers. For the pg_net-side numbers themselves I rely on a sibling verifier's independent live re-query, run 2026-09-05 against the same production project: `SELECT status_code, error_msg IS NOT NULL, count(*) FROM net._http_response GROUP BY 1,2` returned a single row — status_code NULL, had_error true, n=72, spanning the table's entire retention window, every error_msg reading 'Timeout of 20000 ms reached ...'; and `cron.job_run_details` for jobid 2 over the same 24h showed exactly one status group, succeeded=288 — because net.http_post only records the enqueue, never the HTTP outcome. The same verifier pulled the literal cron command and confirmed `timeout_milliseconds := 20000`. Their measured clean-tick activity span (mean 39.2s, max 46.3s, i.e. well past 20s) independently supports this finding's falsification claim that the work is not actually truncated by the client giving up.
verified.impact: Confirmed: nothing downstream of pg_cron can ever observe an HTTP-level failure on the scheduler's only entry point (a bad secret, a 500, a broken deploy), because the response is discarded before pg_cron records anything beyond 'the request was enqueued'.
verified.recommendation: Same as the finder's: raise timeout_milliseconds to comfortably exceed the 60s maxDuration (e.g. 65000), or have POST /api/cron return 202 immediately and process asynchronously so a real status code is captured quickly either way.
verified.note: The two in-repo numbers (maxDuration=60, TIME_BUDGET_MS=50000) I confirmed myself directly from source. The pg_net-side numbers (20000ms timeout, 72/72 timed-out responses, 288/288 falsely-succeeded run details) I could not query myself this session (Supabase MCP unavailable) and instead rely on an independent live re-verification performed days earlier against the same production database, which reproduced them essentially exactly.

verified.title: cron.job_run_details holds ~46-47 MB of unpruned run history for one 5-minute job and is structurally invisible to autovacuum
verified.evidence: This finding is a pure live-database-state claim with no code correlate to check directly (there is no purge job anywhere in the repo, which I confirmed by grepping the migrations directory for any DELETE against cron.job_run_details — none exists). I could not query pg_class/pg_stat_all_tables for this table myself this session. A sibling verifier independently re-ran the same measurement on 2026-09-05 against the same production project: count=29,550 rows (oldest 2026-05-25), live_data=16 MB, on_disk=47 MB (66% waste — matching this finding's 46MB/19.1%-of-DB framing almost exactly), vacuum_count=0, autovacuum_count=0, last_autovacuum=NULL, pg_class.relpages=0/reltuples=-1 (never analyzed) — every one of those matches this finding's cited numbers within the drift expected over a few days of continued 288-runs/day growth, and independently derives the same ~165-166 MB/year growth-rate projection.
verified.impact: Confirmed: this is real, measured, unpruned bloat that autovacuum structurally cannot reach (pg_cron's launcher writes rows without incrementing the table's insert statistics), corroborated by an independent audit of the same table days apart showing the same non-vacuuming behavior and a consistent size trajectory.
verified.recommendation: Same as the finder's: schedule a daily purge (`DELETE FROM cron.job_run_details WHERE end_time < now() - interval '7 days'`) and run one VACUUM (FULL) to reclaim the existing bloat, since ordinary autovacuum will never fire here.
verified.note: Could not be queried directly by me this session (Supabase MCP unavailable); verdict rests on an independent live re-verification performed days earlier against the same production database, whose numbers (47MB, 66% waste, zero autovacuum activity, ~165MB/yr growth) match this finding closely enough to treat as reproduced.

verified.title: The typed job claim's `($2 IS NULL OR type=$2)` predicate is non-sargable and the only pending-row index (idx_job_queue_pick) has no `type` column, so a low-priority claim walks and heap-fetches the whole higher-priority backlog
verified.evidence: I read lib/jobs/db.ts:30-49 myself: the predicate `AND ($2::text IS NULL OR type = $2)` is at line 40 exactly as cited, inside a query ordered `priority DESC, run_at ASC`. I independently confirmed the index shape from the migration itself rather than trusting the finder's description of it: supabase/migrations/20260526120000_041_job_queue.sql:55-57 defines `idx_job_queue_pick ON job_queue (priority DESC, run_at ASC) WHERE status='pending'` — no `type` column, exactly as claimed, so a typed claim cannot be served by an index seek on type and must filter post-scan. A sibling verifier independently ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the live claim query on 2026-09-05: for a low-priority type it showed `Filter: (type = ...), Rows Removed by Filter: 19731, Buffers: shared hit=10815`, and separately pulled the same pg_stat_statements entry this finding cites, getting 22,574 calls / 91,754,087 shared blocks / 4,065 blocks-per-call lifetime average — closely matching this finding's own pg_stat_statements pull of 21,255 calls / 83,400,706 blocks / 3,924 blocks-per-call (two snapshots days apart, both describing the same real, large, and growing cost).
verified.impact: Confirmed as a real and large cost, though the sibling verifier adds a useful nuance worth carrying forward: 3,900-4,065 blocks/call is closer to the honest PRODUCTION AVERAGE than the theoretical worst case, because the query walks `priority DESC` from the front, so a high-priority type (e.g. mpesa_reconcile at priority 10) is found almost immediately while a low-priority type (e.g. sms_release_stale_reservations at priority 3) pays close to the full backlog scan (they measured up to 10,815 blocks for that case). Either way this is tens of gigabytes of daily buffer traffic and it scales linearly with the very backlog that finding 3 shows is growing by 1,700+ rows/day.
verified.recommendation: Same as the finder's: add a composite index on (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending' and split the claim into typed/untyped statements instead of the OR-form predicate.
verified.note: The predicate location and the missing-column index shape were both confirmed directly by my own read of the source and the migration. The exact live block-count magnitude I could not re-query myself this session (Supabase MCP unavailable) but it was independently reproduced within about 3% by a sibling verifier days earlier against the same table.

verified.title: The tick's two introspection queries (getDistinctPendingTypes + getQueueDepth) cost roughly 2.1s/tick and 62h/year — OVERSTATED: a contemporaneous independent re-measurement puts the real, non-double-counted cost at ~0.95s/tick (~27h/year), about 2.3x smaller
verified.evidence: I confirmed all three queries exist exactly as cited: lib/jobs/db.ts:57-66 (getDistinctPendingTypes), lib/jobs/db.ts:89-111 (getQueueDepth), and the resetStuckJobs UPDATE, called in that order from lib/jobs/processor.ts:133 (resetStuckJobs), :142 (emitQueueDepth -> getQueueDepth), and :144 (getDistinctPendingTypes) — so getQueueDepth genuinely runs BEFORE getDistinctPendingTypes on every tick, not after. A sibling verifier independently re-differenced pg_stat_statements for both queries against the finder's own snapshot on 2026-09-05: getDistinctPendingTypes' real marginal cost came out to ~15.1ms/call (not the ~856ms lifetime-mean figure this finding uses), because the 121-day lifetime average the finder quoted is dominated by a historical CPU-contention period and does not describe current behaviour (shared_blks_read=0 in their fresh EXPLAIN — no disk I/O either way). getQueueDepth's marginal cost, by contrast, DID reproduce as genuinely expensive: ~930.6ms/call, essentially matching this finding's own 1,259.5ms figure once the same double-counting correction is applied. The sibling verifier's explicit conclusion: 'the finder billed getQueueDepth AND getDistinctPendingTypes and summed them to "2.1s of introspection per tick". That double-counts. The two run back-to-back over the same rows, and only the FIRST pays: ~931ms for getQueueDepth, then ~15ms for getDistinctPendingTypes.' Real introspection cost per tick is therefore ~0.95s, not 2.1s: 0.95s x 288 ticks/day = ~274s/day = ~4.6 min/day = ~28h/year, versus this finding's claimed 611s/day / 62h/year.
verified.impact: The qualitative point stands (real DB time is spent every tick before any job is claimed, and it is dominated by a full-backlog scan that both fixes described elsewhere in this dimension would eliminate), but the magnitude used to justify it is roughly 2.3x too large because it double-charges a query pair that in practice shares one expensive scan, not two.
verified.recommendation: Do not cite '2.1s/tick, 62h/year' going forward — cite ~0.95s/tick (~27-28h/year), almost entirely attributable to getQueueDepth. The finder's own recommendation (merge the two queries into one GROUP BY, and/or downgrade emitQueueDepth to run less than every tick) is still correct and becomes even more clearly worthwhile once the dedup-key fix (finding 3) shrinks the backlog these queries scan.
verified.note: OVERSTATED: the shape and existence of both queries and their call order were confirmed directly from source by me. The ~2.1s/62h magnitude is corrected down to ~0.95s/~27-28h by an independent live re-measurement performed days earlier against the same production database, which specifically identified and explained the double-counting error (getDistinctPendingTypes benefits from the buffer cache getQueueDepth just warmed, so only the first of the two pays the real cost).
